documents.content: Rooms — Construction, Geometry, and System Integration A room is the fundamental spatial unit of the Creatures 3 world. Every metaroom is built out of rooms; every door connects exactly one or two rooms; every CA value lives in a room; every agent lives in (or floats above) a room; and almost every navigation, perception, and physics decision the engine makes ultimately bottoms out at "which room is this?". This article is a deep-dive on the room object itself — how it gets built, what fields it carries, how it connects to its neighbours, and how those connections feed both the map system (creature navigation, doors, links) and the cellular-automata system (proteins, smells, home markers, environmental conditions). For the broader hierarchical context of metarooms, see World Map System. For the rules governing CA values themselves, see Cellular Automata System. What a Room Is In the JS rebuild a room is a single instance of . Its identity is just a numeric ; everything else is data attached to that id. Rooms live in (a ) and additionally belong to exactly one parent metaroom via . Conceptually, a room is four edges and a slab of CA: A room is not a fixed-size grid cell. The constructor seeds defaults from a 144×150 grid bucket ( ) but those values are overwritten almost immediately by or once the actual coordinates from the CAOS command are known. The grid coordinates linger as / and are used for spatial bucketing, not for geometry. Construction Lifecycle Rooms are created exclusively through ( ). This is the JS equivalent of the original engine's room-creation routine and is invoked by the CAOS command, which in turn is invoked from bootstrap scripts like . The full sequence of an call is: Bounds check. is enforced ( ). The metaroom must already exist ( ). construction. A new object is allocated with sequential id . The constructor populates default boundaries from the grid bucket and zero-fills 20 CA values ( ). Geometry application. If the room is rectangular (all four corner Y values are equal) is called; otherwise — for sloped floors or ceilings — is called instead ( ). Both methods rebuild the four corner points ( , , , ) and recompute . See Room Geometry. Activation. and mark the room ready for simulation ( ). Storage. The room is inserted into and registered with its parent metaroom ( ). Display registration. adds the room to the rendering planes if a is attached ( ). Door creation. ( ) walks the four edges of the new room and finds overlaps with existing sibling rooms in the same metaroom. For each overlap it either creates a brand-new shared or mutates an existing sibling's external door into a shared one. This is where the door segmentation pipeline runs — see Door Segmentation. Navigable-door computation for the new room. ( ) walks and promotes at most one door to and at most one to . See Navigable Door Promotion. Refresh of affected siblings. ( ) iterates the new room's horizontal shared doors and re-runs the promotion pass on every sibling whose door was just upgraded from external ( ) to shared ( ). Without this step a sibling's / would still reflect its pre-merge state and would never see the new connection. Mirrors the explicit left/right neighbour refresh loops in the original engine. The complete call chain for steps 7–9: Order matters. Rooms can be added in any geometric order (right-of, left-of, top-of, etc.), and the segmentation pipeline must produce identical world topology regardless. The previous JS implementation didn't always honour that — see Parent Ordering Convention for the convention that makes order-independence work. Room Geometry A room's footprint is described by four corner points plus their deltas. Both rectangular and sloped rooms use the same four-point representation; rectangular rooms simply have horizontal and lines. Vector fields The legacy scalar accessors , , , , , , , ( , , ) are kept in sync for backward compatibility but should be considered derived state — write through / , not by hand. Rectangular vs sloped rooms Rectangular — all four corner Y values are equal pairs ( , ). Created by ( ). The floor and ceiling lines are exactly horizontal. Sloped — at least one of or . Created by ( ). The floor and/or ceiling line carries a slope; the AABB is computed from the min/max of all four corner Y values. picks the right method automatically based on whether ( ). Perimeter length Used as the denominator in the door doorage formula (see Permeability): Computed by ( ) and re-run automatically inside / . Mirrors the original engine's perimeter computation. For a rectangular 100×50 room this collapses to . Sloped rooms contribute the actual slanted lengths via . Room Types Every room has a (and equivalent alias ) in the range ( in ). Types are assigned via the CAOS command, almost always immediately after the corresponding : Room type is not geometry — it's a selector into the CA rates table. returns a triple ( ), and that triple is what governs how each CA evolves in this room. Different room types (e.g. "outdoor jungle floor" vs "norn home" vs "vehicle interior") get different rate profiles loaded by commands during bootstrap, so the same CA index can behave very differently depending on which physical region of the world you're in. Two room types in the standard rate table are particularly notable for navigable CAs: Types 11–15 have for CA15 (Norn Home) and friends — they're CA-opaque dead zones. Vehicle interiors and sealed regions live here. Types 5–7 have (vs for normal indoor types). They still propagate but with reduced source strength. A complete CA15 rate table is included in the Cellular Automata System article. Door Collections A room's connections to the rest of the world are stored in five collections, of which only three are routinely used by the map and CA systems: is the source of truth. and are promoted references — they always point at members of , never at independent objects. The four directional sub-collections ( ) are convenience filters maintained by and friends. Door anatomy A ( ) carries the following state: Two of these fields are subtle and worth their own sections: (which decides whether the door can ever become navigable) and / (which encode a geometric ordering convention the rest of the engine depends on). is for horizontal walking doors — the primary mechanism by which a creature walks from one room to another along the floor chain. is for vertical doors — ceiling doors, floor doors, hatches, ladder mouths, etc. Only doors are eligible for promotion to / . Vertical doors live in and participate in non-navigable CA diffusion, but they never carry navigable CAs and they never become navigable for creature pathing. Parent ordering convention The engine — both the original and the JS rebuild — enforces this rule for every shared door ( ): is the geometrically LEFT room (for horizontal doors) or TOP room (for vertical doors). is the geometrically RIGHT or BOTTOM room. This is not a soft suggestion. Multiple downstream systems read to mean "the room on this door's left/top side": checks only when the current room is , and only when the current room is . If parents are in the wrong order, neither branch matches and the door silently fails promotion. literally treats as "the room to the left" when iterating navigable CA propagation along the room chain. The pathfinding/floor-chain code at / is computed from the same parent-order assumption. The JS door-creation pipeline enforces the convention through a dedicated helper ( ): It's invoked from the two real shared-door creation sites: and 's overlap-segment construction. Mirrors the original engine's room-edge routine, which has the same branching inline. A door created without honouring this convention will look perfectly fine in the door inspector — same parents, same coordinates, same permeability — but will be invisible to navigable CA propagation and to floor-chain navigation. This was a long-lived bug in the JS rebuild before being fixed; see Common Pitfalls. Door Segmentation When a new room is added to a metaroom that already contains rooms, its edges may partially overlap existing rooms' external doors. The engine handles this with a one-pass segmentation algorithm in + ( , ). This is the JS equivalent of the original engine's room-edge routine. For each sibling door that overlaps the new room's edge, produces 1, 2, or 3 segments: The first segment mutates the existing door object in place ( ). Subsequent segments call ( ) to allocate brand-new doors. After the loop, ( ) creates unshared external doors for any portion of the new room's edge that wasn't covered by any sibling. The shared overlap segment is the one that needs the parent-ordering convention applied. Before applying parents, the segment is built like this: here is the edge of the new room being processed (not the sibling). The helper resolves which of the two ids should be based on whether the new room is on the left/top side or the right/bottom side of the resulting door. Segments 1 and 3 inherit parent ordering Segments 1 and 3 (the non-overlapping leftover bits of the existing door) preserve / . As long as the existing door was created via the fixed shared-door path or as an external door (which is a different convention; see below), the leftover segments inherit a coherent ordering automatically. Unshared (external) doors Unshared doors ( ) sit in exactly one room. They are created by ( ) or and use the JS-internal convention for all directions — not the geometric convention used for shared doors. This divergence from the original engine is intentional and harmless: external doors have , which fails the very first filter in , so they never get inspected for navigability and their parent slots are never read by anything that cares about the convention. If an unshared door is later upgraded into a shared door via , the segmentation code overwrites and with the correctly-ordered helper output — so the internal convention for unshared doors never leaks into a shared door. Permeability Every door has an integer in , set initially by door creation (shared doors default to , unshared/external doors default to ) and modifiable at runtime by the CAOS command: Permeability has two completely different effective formulas, one for each CA update path. See Cellular Automata System for the full picture; the room-side summary is: Non-navigable doorage (cached) For non-navigable CAs (sound, light, heat, water, …) the per-tick equilibrium pipeline uses a squared, length-weighted, perimeter-normalised doorage value, computed once per door by ( ) and stored on the door as (as seen from room A) and (as seen from room B): This is also where comes from — the sum over all doors and links touching the room of that side's doorage, clamped to 1 ( , ). enters the per-tick update at : i.e. a room with leaky walls keeps less of its own equilibrium temp value because more of it leaked out through doors during phase 2. The squared term means a door at permeability 50 transmits only 25% as much non-navigable CA as one at permeability 100. Navigable per-hop attenuation For navigable CAs (proteins, smells, home markers, …) the recursive walk in uses a raw, per-hop factor: Length and perimeter don't enter at all. There's no squaring. A single hop through a door at permeability 50 with diffusion 0.9 on both sides gives of the source's contribution at that hop. Practical consequences for room authoring A non-navigable CA care about how long the door is and how big the receiving room is. Big rooms with small doors retain more of their own CA. A navigable CA only cares about permeability and the two diffusion rates, and it travels recursively up to hops in a single propagation pass. Setting cuts both CA paths instantly. Setting is the maximum; there is no "more open than wide open". Navigable Door Promotion This is the most easily misunderstood aspect of the room system, and it's the source of most "my CA value is mysteriously zero in the next room" bugs. A door becomes a navigable door for a particular room only if decides to promote it. The function walks and applies three filters to each door: — external ( ) doors are never navigable. ( ) — vertical doors and hatches are never navigable. Floor-edge alignment. The room's floor endpoint must coincide with the neighbour's floor endpoint within 2.0 units in both x and y: is set when in both axes (and ). is set when in both axes (and ). The 2.0-unit tolerance is a JS-side relaxation of the original engine's exact equality. Anything the original engine considers floor-aligned, JS also accepts. The check depends on the parent-ordering convention described earlier: it asks "if I'm parent1, does my right floor corner touch the other room's left floor corner?" — which is only a meaningful question when is actually the left room. Get the parent ordering wrong and both branches fail the geometry test no matter how perfectly the rooms are aligned. What "navigable" means downstream A door pointed at by / is the only door type that: Carries navigable CA propagation (proteins, smells, home markers) via . Doors that live only in are completely ignored by navigable CAs even at permeability 100. Defines the horizontal floor chain that creatures walk along when traversing a metaroom. The Room fields / are derived from the same scan. If you want a navigable CA to flow across a connection that isn't a horizontal floor-aligned door — a vertical hatch between two metarooms, a teleporter, a vehicle dock, anything where the floor endpoints don't touch — the answer is to add a , not to fight the navigable-door promotion. Links live in , are walked unconditionally by phase A of , and don't care about floor geometry — they only care about their own permeability and the two rooms' diffusion rates. Refresh after is called on the newly-added room from inside . But that's not enough on its own: when a new room overlaps an existing room's external door, the existing door is mutated in place to become a shared door, and the existing room's navigable pointers were computed back when its door was still external (and was rejected by filter #1). Without an explicit refresh, the existing room would never re-see the upgraded connection. ( ) closes this loop. After finishes building the new room, it walks the new room's horizontal shared doors, dedupes the other-room ids, and re-runs on each affected sibling. Mirrors the explicit left/right neighbour refresh loops in the original engine. There's also a fallback recompute in the deserialisation path ( ): It fires when restoring a room from a saved world if either pointer is missing, repairing half-restored states. (An older form of this guard tested instead of , which silently skipped recompute on rooms with one resolved pointer and one missing one — a latent bug that's been corrected.) Cellular Automata Storage on the Room Every room carries its own slab of CA state, all of it allocated in the constructor ( ): is the public observable for CA index and is what every reader ( , , the room debugger, etc.) consults. Everything else is internal scratch state for the CA update pipeline. Two important invariants: is never decayed for navigable indices. For navigable CAs the value is a persistent accumulating sum maintained by . There is no per-tick equilibrium loop touching it. Removing or killing every emitter for a navigable index leaves all reachable rooms at whatever delta the emitters last pushed in, until something else mutates it. is recomputed every tick for non-navigable indices by the round-robin equilibrium loop. Specifically, each call to selects one CA index, runs to derive a new from , sets , then phase 2 redistributes between rooms via , and phase 3 finally adds back . The full algorithm — and the navigable / non-navigable split — is documented in Cellular Automata System. Where agent emissions land Emissions enter rooms from two paths ( ): Non-navigable emissions call ( ) which adds to the room's only on the CA's turn in the round-robin. Off-cycle ticks do nothing. Navigable emissions call ( ) which propagates a delta through the link/navigable-door network from the source room out to a maximum of 30 hops. Each room visited gets its incremented by the attenuated delta. The agent re-runs this only when it changes room (one negative call from the old room, one positive call from the new one). Either way, the room is the deposit target. Nothing in the CA system writes to a "world" or a "metaroom" — everything is per-room. Connection With the Map System Beyond CA storage, a room is the unit of: Agent containment is a of every agent currently inside the room ( ). Agents are assigned by / during their physics update based on which room contains the agent's position. Most engine queries that need "what's in this room" go through this set. Neighbour tracking Two parallel structures track room-to-room adjacency: Direction constants for the buckets are ( ). Doors maintain these via whenever a shared door is created or mutated. Note that the navigable system ( / , / ) is separate from the directional neighbour buckets. A room can have multiple horizontal neighbours in / while only one of them is the floor-aligned navigable neighbour. Pathfinding and navigable CAs use the navigable pointers; vision casts and bulk neighbour queries use the buckets. Room-pair lookups is a ( ) indexed by sorted room id pair. It lets answer "which doors connect these two rooms?" in O(1). Maintained by , , and the deserialisation path. Links — the escape hatch is the home of explicitly-created objects ( ), one of which can join two rooms regardless of their geometric relationship. Created by the CAOS command, populated from PRAY data, and walked by phase A of . Use links when: Two rooms need to exchange navigable CAs but their floors don't touch (separate metarooms, vertical shafts, teleporters). Two rooms need to be navigation-equivalent for some specific subsystem without forcing a full geometric merge. Links have their own field and respect both rooms' rates during navigable CA propagation, identically to navigable doors. Common Pitfalls and Debugging A short cheat sheet for the most common room-system confusions. "My CA value is zero in this room" Walk the seven-step checklist in Cellular Automata System → Debugging Zero Values. The most common causes, in order: The bootstrap script that emits this CA never ran (or its agents got killed). The source room's for this CA is 0 — the room type at the emitter's position has no line covering this index. The path between the source room and the destination is broken — check for any link or door, or any room with , along the way. The relevant door isn't promoted to navigable even though the rooms are floor-aligned — see next item. "The door connecting these rooms shows but the navigable indicator is " That door is in but failed promotion to / . The Map debugger ( ) shows the precise reason in the Navigable row tooltip; it will be one of: — the door isn't shared. Should have been merged with a sibling at room-creation time but wasn't. — the door is vertical. Use a if you need navigable CA flow across this connection. — the floor corners aren't within 2.0 units of each other. Either the rooms genuinely aren't floor-aligned (in which case use a ), or the geometry data is off by a small numeric error. "The door is navigable on one side but not the other" The Map debugger labels this . It means but (or vice versa). In a freshly built world this should be impossible — the promotion code is symmetric — but it can occur in: Saved worlds restored before the fallback guard was widened from to . Old rooms whose siblings were added by an that didn't run . Force-reloading the world or calling on the half-wired side fixes it. "I changed at runtime but the CA didn't change" For navigable CAs, the cached propagation deltas don't recompute when permeability changes — they were applied at the moment the emitter started emitting and are now sitting as raw deposits in . The standard approach is to re-emit (toggle the emitter off and back on, or move the emitter through a room cycle) to force to recalculate the chain. For non-navigable CAs the change takes effect on the next round-robin pass for that CA index. "I added a room and now a different room's is wrong" Make sure is calling for the new room. If you're wiring up rooms via a custom path (test harness, manual instantiation, world deserialisation), you must mirror what does in steps 7–9 — , then on the new room, then the same on every sibling now sharing a horizontal door with it. "ADDR returns a room id but the room isn't visible" and are called from ( ) — verify both are true. is the display flag ( ); check if rendering looks empty. Note that and ( ) gate the room overlay independently of the room being active. documents.content: Day/Night Cycle, Seasons, and Time System Overview Creatures 3 uses a tick-based time system where all temporal values -- time of day, season, day within season, and years elapsed -- are derived on-the-fly from a single counter: the world tick ( in the original engine, in JS). There are no separate hour, minute, or day member variables. Every time a CAOS script or engine system needs to know the time, it is computed from the current tick using the world's time configuration. This design comes directly from the original engine. World Tick The world tick is an unsigned 32-bit integer that increments by 1 each game tick, as long as the world is not paused. The default tick interval is 50ms, giving 20 ticks per second. The world tick is the single source of truth for all time calculations. Time Configuration Four configurable values control the time system. They are set to defaults in the World constructor and can be changed at runtime via GAME variables and the RGAM command. Variable Engine Name Default Description ---------- ---------- --------- ------------- 20 Real-world minutes per game day 3 Game days per season 4 Number of seasons per year 12 Computed: The corresponding GAME variables are: These can be set by bootstrap scripts and take effect when is called. Tick-to-Time Conversions All time calculations start from a common formula for ticks per day: With defaults, one game day = 20 real minutes, one season = 60 real minutes, one year = 4 real hours. Time of Day The day is divided into 5 equal periods (the constant): Value Period Tick Range (default) ------- -------- --------------------- 0 Dawn 0 -- 4,799 1 Morning 4,800 -- 9,599 2 Afternoon 9,600 -- 14,399 3 Evening 14,400 -- 19,199 4 Night 19,200 -- 23,999 Each period lasts = 4,800 ticks = 4 real minutes with default settings. Algorithm The original algorithm iterates backwards from Night to Dawn: The JS implementation in replicates this exactly. Seasons The year is divided into equal seasons (default 4): Value Season Day Range Tick Range (default) ------- -------- ----------- --------------------- 0 Spring Days 0-2 0 -- 71,999 1 Summer Days 3-5 72,000 -- 143,999 2 Autumn Days 6-8 144,000 -- 215,999 3 Winter Days 9-11 216,000 -- 287,999 Algorithm The original algorithm uses the same backward-iteration pattern: Day Within Season returns which day of the current season it is (0 to ): With defaults, this returns 0, 1, or 2. Years Elapsed returns the total number of complete game years since world creation: CAOS Commands Time Query Commands Command Returns Example Value --------- --------- --------------- Time of day (0-4) 2 (Afternoon) Season (0-3) 1 (Summer) Day within current season (0 to seasonLengthInDays-1) 2 Years elapsed since world creation 0 Current world tick (saved with world) 48000 Engine tick (NOT saved, resets on restart) 120000 Real-world day of month (system clock) 15 Real-world month (system clock) 7 Time Control Command Usage Description --------- ------- ------------- Command Pause world ticks (days, seasons, delayed messages all stop) Command Resume world ticks RV Returns 1 if paused, 0 if running Historical Time Queries These return what the time was at a specific past tick, using the same algorithms with an explicit tick value: Command Usage Returns --------- ------- --------- Query past season Season at that tick Query past day-in-season Day at that tick Query past year Year at that tick Environmental Effects The time of day drives room environmental properties updated each tick in : Light Levels Time of Day Light Level ------------- ------------- Dawn 0.5 Morning 0.9 Afternoon 1.0 Evening 0.6 Night 0.2 Temperature Temperature varies around a base of 0.5, offset by time of day: Time of Day Offset Temperature ------------- -------- ------------- Dawn +0.00 0.50 Morning +0.10 0.60 Afternoon +0.20 0.70 Evening +0.05 0.55 Night -0.15 0.35 These values feed into the CA (Cellular Automata) system, which diffuses them between connected rooms. Implementation Files File Purpose ------ --------- , , , , , CAOS TIME command CAOS SEAN command CAOS DATE command CAOS YEAR command CAOS WPAU command CAOS WTIK command CAOS ETIK command Historical season query Historical day-in-season query Historical year query Quick Reference With default settings (20-min day, 3-day season, 4 seasons): Unit Duration (real time) Duration (ticks) ------ --------------------- ------------------- 1 time-of-day period 4 minutes 4,800 1 game day 20 minutes 24,000 1 season 60 minutes 72,000 1 year 4 hours 288,000

documents.content: Agent-Room Collision System Implementation Overview The agent-room collision system is a sophisticated physics engine that prevents agents from passing through room boundaries (doors) while enabling natural movement behaviors like sliding along walls, bouncing off surfaces, and navigating corners. The system has been fully ported from the original Creatures 3 engine to JavaScript, maintaining architectural fidelity while leveraging modern web capabilities. Location: Primary Method: System Architecture Core Components The collision system consists of six integrated phases, each building upon the previous: Phase 1: Foundation - Geometric Collision Detection Purpose Establish the core mathematical algorithms for detecting when and where collisions occur. Key Methods Purpose: Tests if two line segments intersect and calculates intersection point. Algorithm: Based on parametric line equations Returns: if no intersection if intersection detected : How far along the first segment (0-1) : Exact intersection coordinates : Position along second segment (0-1) Purpose: Efficiently finds which rooms the movement path crosses. Algorithm: AABB Culling: Calculate bounding box of path Quick Rejection: Skip rooms that don't intersect bounding box Detailed Test: Check if path actually crosses room boundaries Returns: Array of Room objects that the path crosses Purpose: Tests if a line segment passes through a room. Algorithm: Check if either endpoint is inside room Test path against all 4 room edges using Returns: Boolean indicating if path intersects room Phase 2: Diamond Model - Natural Sliding Movement Purpose Replace point-based collision with a diamond-shaped agent model that enables smooth sliding along walls. The Diamond Shape Agents are represented as a diamond with 4 vertices based on their width and height: Key Method Purpose: Creates a 4-vertex diamond shape and selects 3 vertices facing the movement direction. Algorithm: Why 3 Vertices? Diagonal movement exposes 2 vertices (e.g., right + bottom when moving down-right) System adds 1 more vertex to ensure coverage Testing 3 vertices provides accurate collision detection without excessive computation Enhanced Collision Detection Purpose: Tests agent's diamond vertices against all room doors. Algorithm: Calculate diamond vertices based on movement direction Find rooms along path using AABB culling For each room's doors: Skip permeable doors (permeability ≥ threshold) For each vertex: Calculate vertex movement path Test against door using Track closest collision Return collision info with earliest time value Returns: if no collision Collision object with: Phase 3: Multi-Iteration Loop - High-Speed Physics Purpose Handle multiple collisions within a single physics frame, enabling accurate high-speed movement without tunneling. The Problem Without multi-iteration: Ball bouncing in corner processes only 1 bounce per frame High-speed agents can pass through thin walls Physics feels sluggish and inaccurate The Solution Time-Based Iteration Loop Key Features Time Tracking: Each collision consumes a portion of the frame time Remaining time used for subsequent collisions Maximum 10 iterations prevents infinite loops Early Exit Optimization: Example Scenario: Phase 4: Advanced Collision Response - Realistic Physics Purpose Apply physically accurate collision responses based on surface type and collision angle. Collision Response Dispatcher Purpose: Routes to appropriate physics algorithm based on collision type. Algorithm: Geometric Energy Loss (Walls/Ceilings) Purpose: Applies physically accurate energy loss during wall bounces. Algorithm (Ported from the original engine): Why This Works: Geometric method more accurate than simple multiplication Energy loss proportional to collision severity Handles glancing blows vs direct hits naturally Floor Sliding Physics Purpose: Projects velocity and gravity onto floor slope for realistic sliding. Algorithm: Key Behaviors: Steep slopes: Agent slides down Gentle slopes: Static friction stops movement Friction: Gradually slows sliding Phase 5: Vertex/Corner Handling - No Sticking Purpose Handle collisions at corners and vertices to prevent agents from getting stuck. The Problem Agents hitting exact corner points can get stuck Velocity becomes zero at sharp angles Navigation feels unnatural Corner Detection Purpose: Calculates reflection when agent hits a vertex where two doors meet. Algorithm: Corner Types Sharp Corner (< 90°): Gentle Corner (≥ 90°): Supporting Methods Purpose: Locates all doors sharing a vertex point. Algorithm: Purpose: Calculates angle between two door direction vectors. Algorithm: Integration with Agent Physics Agent.js Integration The collision system integrates with Agent physics through the method: Physics Parameters Agent Properties: , : Agent dimensions for diamond calculation : Minimum door permeability to pass through (0-100) : Energy retained on bounce (0-1) : No bounce (sticky) : Half energy retained : Perfect elastic collision : Air resistance (0-1) : No air resistance : Typical value (5% velocity loss per second) : Sliding friction (0-1) : No friction : Typical value : Acceleration (pixels/second²) Default: Performance Characteristics Computational Complexity Per Physics Update: Room lookup: O(R) where R = rooms along path (typically 1-3) AABB culling reduces this significantly Door testing: O(D) where D = doors per room (typically 4) Vertex testing: O(V) where V = 3 vertices Total: O(R × D × V) ≈ O(36) operations typical Iteration Count: Stationary agents: 0 iterations (early exit) Normal movement: 1-2 iterations Bouncing: 3-5 iterations High-speed corner: Up to 10 iterations max Optimization Techniques AABB Culling: Quick rejection of distant rooms Early Exit: Stop when velocity < threshold Iteration Limiting: Max 10 collisions per frame Permeability Filtering: Skip passable doors immediately Map-Based Lookups: O(1) door retrieval Performance Monitoring Testing and Validation Test Scenarios Basic Movement: ✅ Agent stops at impermeable door ✅ Agent passes through permeable door ✅ Agent slides along angled wall Bouncing Physics: ✅ Ball bounces off wall with energy loss ✅ Multiple bounces in corner within one frame ✅ Agent comes to rest naturally Floor Behavior: ✅ Slides down steep slope ✅ Stops on gentle slope (static friction) ✅ Friction slows movement Corner Navigation: ✅ Sharp corners bounce agent back ✅ Gentle corners allow smooth sliding ✅ No sticking at vertices High-Speed Movement: ✅ No tunneling through thin walls ✅ Accurate collision at high velocity ✅ Multiple collisions handled correctly Debug Output Enable detailed logging: Future Enhancements Potential Improvements Bidirectional Testing Test door vertices vs agent edges More accurate for edge cases Spatial Partitioning Quadtree for room lookups Beneficial with 500+ rooms Debug Visualization Render collision diamonds Show collision paths and contact points Visual normal vectors Advanced Materials Surface-specific friction Bouncy vs sticky materials Temperature-based properties Summary The agent-room collision system provides: ✅ Accurate Collision Detection: Diamond model with multi-vertex testing ✅ Realistic Physics: Geometric energy loss and vector projection ✅ High-Speed Support: Multi-iteration loop prevents tunneling ✅ Corner Handling: Spike detection and averaged normal reflection ✅ Performance Optimized: AABB culling and early exit conditions ✅ Original Engine Parity: Direct port of original algorithms The system is production-ready and fully integrated with the agent physics pipeline.

documents.content: Cellular Automata System The Cellular Automata (CA) system simulates 20 environmental properties per room — heat, light, food smells, creature smells, home markers, and so on — and propagates them between rooms through doors and links. There are two completely separate update paths: one for non-navigable CAs (per-tick equilibrium + door diffusion) and one for navigable CAs (immediate recursive propagation from each emitter). Most of the confusion when debugging the CA system comes from not realising which path applies to which CA index. This article explains both. The 20 CA Properties Each room maintains exactly 20 CA values ( ). The names are not read from the catalogue at runtime: exports as the single canonical list (with and, for anything a person reads, — → ), and the debugger, the graph module and the Help Chat's context builder all import it from there. The list is hand-picked to match the C++ entries for chemicals 165-184, which are the same twenty channels as the creature smells them — but those entries are inconsistent (channel 11 has no name, 3 and 5 are both "water", 18 and 19 are blank), hence the tidied names below: Index Name Navigable? ------- ------ ------------ 0 sound no 1 light no 2 heat no 3 water no 4 nutrient no 5 water2 no 6 protein yes 7 carbohydrate yes 8 fat yes 9 flowers no 10 machinery yes 11 creatureSmell1 yes 12 nornSmell yes 13 grendelSmell yes 14 ettinSmell yes 15 nornHome yes 16 grendelHome yes 17 ettinHome yes 18 unused18 yes 19 unused19 no The navigable set is hard-coded as in , matching the original engine's . Note: "Navigable" has nothing to do with whether the CA can flow between rooms. Both navigable and non-navigable CAs can spread room-to-room — they just use very different algorithms. See the next section. Navigable vs Non-Navigable: The Critical Distinction This is the single most important concept in the CA system. Non-navigable CAs — equilibrium model Non-navigable CAs (sound, light, heat, water, nutrient, flowers, etc.) are updated by a per-tick equilibrium loop. Every game tick the system picks one CA index in round-robin order; for that index it: Pulls the room's current value toward an asymptotic target derived from (the sum of agent contributions since the last update for this CA), weighted by the room's (when rising) or (when falling) rate. Diffuses the resulting temp value through every shared door, weighted by both rooms' rates and the door's . Resets to 0, ready for the next cycle. So a non-navigable CA's value is recomputed every cycle from scratch out of . If the input dries up, the value decays to 0 over a few cycles. Agents emit non-navigable CAs by adding to only on the CA's turn in the round-robin ( ). Navigable CAs — accumulating-delta model Navigable CAs (proteins, smells, home markers, …) are never touched by the per-tick equilibrium loop. explicitly skips them at line 316: Instead, the value is an accumulating sum of deltas pushed in by . Each navigable-CA emitter calls once at install time; that call propagates a single delta out from the agent's room, and the resulting value persists in every reached room. The agent re-emits only when it changes room ( ), at which point it subtracts the old delta from the previous room and adds it to the new one. In other words, the field of navigable-CA values across the world is a steady-state snapshot of every currently-active emitter. There is no per-tick decay, no per-tick equilibrium, no involvement. If no chain of links/doors connects an emitter to a room, that room's value for that CA is exactly zero forever. Side-by-side comparison Aspect Non-navigable Navigable --- --- --- Updated each tick? Yes (round-robin, one CA per tick, every 2 ticks) No — only when an emitter calls What represents An equilibrium driven by current input A persistent sum of all reachable emitter contributions How agents emit adds to only on the CA's turn propagates a one-shot delta on emission start / room change Decays without input? Yes (governed by ) No — stays until the emitter stops or moves Diffusion across doors Per-tick two-way mixing Recursive walk at emission time, attenuated per hop Path metric One hop per tick (slow spread) Up to 30 hops in a single recursive walk ( ) Source-room gain matters? Yes — gates how fast it equilibrates Yes — multiplies the delta at the source (and only there) Destination-room gain matters? Yes (own equilibrium) No (only diffusion enters the propagation factor) Non-Navigable Update Algorithm runs once every two game ticks and processes one CA index per call, cycling 0 → 19. For non-navigable indices it executes the original two-phase algorithm faithfully. Phase 1 — Room equilibrium For each room ( ): The asymptotic transform means a single agent contribution of produces an effective target of ; you need infinite input to ever reach . This prevents a single shouting agent from saturating a CA. Phase 2 — Door and link diffusion For each door and each link with two parents ( ): Each door redistributes a fraction of both rooms' temp values toward their average, weighted by the door's (see Doorage and Permeability). Phase 3 — Final application After all doors have contributed, each room adds back its own retained share ( ): is the sum of all door+link doorages on the room, clamped to . A room with no openings keeps 100% of its temp value; a room with very leaky walls keeps almost none. Combined with phase 2 this gives the room exactly one "unit" of its temp value distributed between itself and its neighbours. Navigable Update Algorithm — When an agent starts emitting a navigable CA — or when it walks into a different room while emitting — the engine calls: Implementation ( ): Three things to notice immediately: is read from the source room only — the room the emitter is sitting in. The destination rooms' gain values are completely ignored. The delta is then multiplied by before being walked outward. Propagation runs to a maximum of link/door hops. Recursive walk : Deposit: . Phase A — links (manual room-to-room connections): for each entry in other than the one we came in on, recurse into the other room with Phase B — iterative left walk along . Each step multiplies by and stops on , no neighbour, or when runs out. At each step it also recursively walks any links attached to the current "left" room (using the pre-advance rates, matching the original engine). Phase C — iterative right walk along , symmetric to phase B. Critical: only follows three channels — , , and . Regular doors in are completely ignored by navigable CA propagation, even at permeability 100. This matches the original engine exactly: non-navigable diffusion uses , but navigable propagation walks only the horizontal "room chain" through the navigable-door pointers and any explicit links. See How a door becomes navigable below. The full propagation factor along a path is therefore: Notes: is the per-hop scaling (permeability is stored as 0–100). It is not squared here — that squaring only applies to non-navigable doorage (see below). Diffusion is multiplied raw, not by its square root, so it attenuates faster than non-navigable diffusion does. uses additive deposits ( ). When an agent moves rooms, first calls the function with from the old room and then from the new room, so the world state stays consistent. Important runtime detail: an emitter does not push every tick. It pushes its delta exactly once at time and again only when it changes room ( — → ). So a navigable-CA value in a room is the algebraic sum of every emitter currently within 30 hops, attenuated by their respective paths. That's why removing or killing every emitter for a CA leaves all reachable rooms at 0 immediately, and why nothing about that value changes between emitter movements. How a door becomes navigable Each room carries two single-pointer fields, and , in addition to the general-purpose . These pointers are the only doors that navigable CAs can cross — so it matters a lot which of a room's doors get promoted to them, and which don't. Promotion is performed by ( , mirroring the original engine). The algorithm walks and applies three filters to each door: — the door connects exactly two rooms. External edges ( ) never become navigable. ( ) — the door is a horizontal walking door. Vertical doors, hatches, ladders, and staircases all have other values and are never promoted, even if they connect adjacent rooms. Floor-edge alignment — the rooms' floor corners must coincide within 2.0 units in both x and y. The exact comparison is asymmetric and depends on the door's parent slots: is set when and . is set when and . (The 2.0-unit tolerance is a JS-side relaxation of the strict equality in the original engine. Anything the original accepts, JS accepts.) The two branches above only make sense if the door's parent slots already encode a specific geometric meaning, which is the fourth — implicit — requirement: The parent-ordering convention For every shared horizontal door, is the geometrically LEFT room and is the geometrically RIGHT room. This is not a soft suggestion. The promotion check above asks "if I'm , does my right floor corner touch the other room's left floor corner?" — which is only a meaningful question when is actually the room on the left. If a door has its parents in the wrong slots (e.g. because it was created when the left-side room was added after the right-side room and the door-creation pipeline didn't reorder them), the geometry test falls into the wrong branch on both sides and the door silently fails promotion no matter how perfectly its floors line up. The same convention is required by , which literally treats as "the room to the left" when iterating navigable propagation along the room chain ( , matching the original engine). The JS door-creation pipeline enforces the convention through a dedicated helper ( ): It is invoked from the two real shared-door creation sites: ( ) and the overlap-segment branch of ( ). Mirrors the original engine's , which has the same branching inline. (External / unshared doors use a different JS-internal convention regardless of direction. This is harmless because external doors fail filter #1 and are never inspected for navigability. If an external door is later upgraded to shared by , its parent slots are overwritten through the helper, so the unshared convention never leaks into a shared door.) Floor-chain visualisation Refresh after is called on the newly-added room from inside . But that's not enough on its own: when a new room overlaps an existing room's external door, the existing door is mutated in place to become a shared door, and the existing room's navigable pointers were computed back when its door was still external (and was rejected by filter #1). Without an explicit refresh, the existing room would never re-see the upgraded connection — it would stay half-wired forever, and navigable CAs from the old room into the new one would never propagate. ( ) closes this loop. After finishes building the new room, it walks the new room's horizontal shared doors, dedupes the other-room ids, and re-runs on each affected sibling. Mirrors the explicit left/right neighbour refresh loops in the original engine. Consequences worth knowing At most one door in each direction can be navigable. If a room had two horizontal floor-aligned doors meeting the test on its right side, the last one inspected would win. In practice rooms in C3 have at most one horizontal neighbour per side, so this rarely matters — but if you author maps with branching floor chains, only one branch will carry navigable CAs. A room at the end of its chain has only one navigable-door pointer set. That's normal. The other side stays . Manual links bypass the navigable-door restriction. If you need a navigable CA to flow across a non-floor-aligned connection (a teleporter, a vehicle dock, a vertical shaft between two metarooms), create a between the rooms. Links live in , are walked by phase A of the recursive walk, and don't care about floor geometry — only about the link's own and the two rooms' diffusion rates. Doors that fail all three filters are still useful for non-navigable CAs. They live in , get a doorage computed in , and participate in the per-tick equilibrium pipeline for sound, light, heat, water, etc. They just don't carry proteins, smells, or home markers. Deserialisation fallback provides a fallback recompute when restoring rooms from a saved world, in case the navigable-door references didn't deserialise cleanly: The condition fires if either pointer is missing — not only when both are missing — so a half-restored room with one resolved id and one unresolved id still gets repaired. (An older form of this guard tested instead of and silently skipped recompute on partially-wired rooms; that latent bug has been corrected.) For the room-side perspective on construction order, the parent-ordering helper, and the original-engine correspondence, see Rooms — Construction, Geometry, and System Integration. CA Rates Each combination of room type (0–15) and CA property (0–19) has a triple. Rates are stored in . Defaults are zero and initialise every rate to — matching the original engine, which has no built-in defaults at all ( ). Rates only become non-zero when bootstrap CAOS scripts run commands at world install time. A room type that no command has touched cannot accumulate, equilibrate, or propagate any CA at all. This is the most common cause of "my CA is silently zero" bugs — see Debugging. Setting rates from CAOS with no arguments after is a getter and returns packed into a single value. Doorage and Permeability Doors and links carry CA between rooms. Their effective conductance is called doorage and is computed differently for the two algorithms. Door / link permeability Every door and link has a field stored as an integer 0–100: Permeability Meaning --- --- 0 sealed (no CA crosses) 50 half-open 100 fully open Permeability is set by the command and may also be modified by gameplay (e.g. an airlock cycling). Non-navigable doorage ( , ) For each door/link with two parent rooms: A room's is the sum over all attached doors and links of its side's doorage, clamped to . This is what gets used by Phase 2's weighting and Phase 3's retention term. The squaring (matching the original engine) means halving permeability quarters the effective opening. Practical effect: Effective conductance --- --- 0 0 % 25 6.25 % 50 25 % 75 56.25 % 100 100 % Navigable doorage does not use the cached values at all. It uses raw (no squaring), multiplied by the diffusion of both endpoint rooms. For a single hop: So navigable propagation is more sensitive to a door being slightly closed than non-navigable diffusion is, but it does not care about door length or room perimeter. Agent CA Emission State machine ( ) Two important behavioural notes: Navigable emission is event-driven (install / room change / disable), not per-tick. Non-navigable emission is round-robin: an agent only deposits on the tick when the CA system is processing its CA ( , ). Off-cycle ticks do nothing. This is why the per-cycle equilibrium math uses directly — exactly one deposit happens between resets. EMIT command Smell Perception Smells reach the brain via ( ), which reads the current room's and runs each through to translate it into a brain category, then writes it into the smell lobe via . The default mapping ( ) for the home/creature smells is: CA index CA name Smell category --- --- --- 12 nornSmell 36 13 grendelSmell 37 14 ettinSmell 38 15 nornHome 30 16 grendelHome 31 17 ettinHome 32 The genome-defined tract then carries those activations into the matching lobe neurons. There is no engine code anywhere that writes directly — the entire "I am at a home" perception is a chain of: bootstrap-spawned emitter agents → navigable CA propagation → smell lobe → genome tract → stim lobe. Debugging Zero Values When a navigable-CA value in a room is unexpectedly , work through the chain in this order: Are there any emitters at all for this CA? Most navigable CAs are populated by bootstrap-spawned emitter agents (e.g. for CA 15/16/17). Verify the bootstrap script ran and the emitter agents still exist. What is the source room's for this CA? multiplies the delta by first. If the room type at the emitter's coordinates has no line covering this CA, gain is and the delta is annihilated before propagation starts. This is the most common cause. What is the source room's own ? The emitter deposits into its own room first, so the source room should be the highest reading anywhere. If it's too, propagation never started — fix step 2 or check that the emitter agent is actually placed in a valid room ( ). Is there a path of links / navigable doors from the source to your destination? Walk it in the map debugger. Watch for any (closed door / link) — that breaks the chain. The walk only follows , , and ; doors that live only in are not used by navigable CAs. Are the doors along the path actually promoted to navigable doors? This is the trap. A door joining the source room to the next one over may sit in with and still not carry CA15 because it was never promoted to / . Check both sides of the door using the Map debugger's Navigable row, which surfaces the result and the rejection reason in one click: Green "Yes — leftNavigableDoor → Room N" / "rightNavigableDoor → Room N" on both sides → the door is fully promoted, propagation will cross it. Red "No" with a tooltip explaining the rejection — one of , , or . The first two mean the door is structurally ineligible; the third usually means the rooms genuinely aren't floor-aligned. In all three cases the fix is content: either correct the geometry, or add a between the rooms — see How a door becomes navigable. Orange "⚠ asymmetric" → promoted on one side but not the other. In a freshly-built world this should be impossible because reruns the promotion check on every sibling whose door was just upgraded. If you see it, either the world was loaded from a save predating the fix, or some manual code path bypasses and forgets to call the refresh. Force-reloading the world or calling on the half-wired side fixes it. Does any room along the path have for this CA? Because the per-hop factor is , a single zero cancels everything downstream. Again, this is usually a missing line for that room type. Is the path longer than 30 hops? is a hard cap. Could attenuation have rounded the value to display-zero? With permeability 100 and diffusion ~0.9 each side, each hop is ~ , so 30 hops still leaves ~0.2% of source intensity. With permeability 30 and diffusion 0.5 each side, each hop is ~ and a handful of hops kills the signal entirely. For non-navigable CAs the questions are different: check , both rooms' / / , and confirm the agent actually got its turn in the round-robin (i.e. that the agent has been alive for at least 20 ticks / one full cycle). CAOS Commands Reference Command Syntax Description --- --- --- Target agent emits CA (state machine above) Read a room's Add to a room's CA value (raw, no propagation) Set or get a ( , ) rate triple Map a CA to a smell category by classifier Get / set room type (selects which row applies) Get / set door permeability between two rooms System Constants Key Files File Purpose ------ --------- Both update paths (non-navigable per-tick + navigable recursive) , , , , , history arrays CA index → smell category translation , , wrapper, room-change tracking CAOS command CAOS command CAOS command Related Articles World Map System — rooms, doors, links, permeability Stimulus Lobe Architecture — how smells become stim neurons Creature Perception — how creatures read CAs

documents.title: Agent System Overview
documents.description: Introduction to agents, lifecycle, hierarchy, and core properties
documents.tags: agents overview hierarchy lifecycle
documents.content: Agent System Overview Introduction In Creatures 3, an Agent is any interactive object in the game world. Everything from simple background decorations to complex machines and the creatures themselves are implemented as agents. The agent system provides a unified framework for: Positioning and physics - Movement, gravity, collision Rendering - Sprite display, animation, z-ordering Scripting - CAOS scripts for behavior Communication - Messaging between agents Persistence - Saving and loading world state What Can Be an Agent? Agent Type Examples ------------ ---------- Simple objects Food, toys, plants, decorations Machines Lifts, doors, dispensers UI elements Buttons, panels, graphs Vehicles Elevators, submarines, carts Creatures Norns, Grendels, Ettins, Geats System Pointer (mouse cursor) Agent Lifecycle Every agent goes through a defined lifecycle from creation to destruction: Lifecycle States State Description ------- ------------- CREATED Agent instantiated but not yet initialized INITIALIZED called, ready to activate ACTIVE called, processing updates INACTIVE called, paused GARBAGE Marked for deletion, no longer valid DELETED Memory freed Class Hierarchy The agent system uses inheritance to provide specialized behavior for different agent types: Inheritance Chain Class Extends Purpose ------- --------- --------- Agent - Base class with physics, messaging, scripting SimpleAgent Agent Single-sprite agent PointerAgent SimpleAgent User cursor with pickup/drop CompoundAgent Agent Multi-part agent with UI support Vehicle CompoundAgent Carries passengers Skeleton Agent Articulated body (creatures) Creature Skeleton Full AI with brain, biochemistry Agent Type Flags Each agent has a type bitmask for efficient type checking. These flags match the original engine: Type Flag Combinations Agent Class Type Flags Bitmask ------------- ------------ --------- SimpleAgent NORMAL \ SIMPLE 3 PointerAgent NORMAL \ SIMPLE \ POINTER 7 CompoundAgent NORMAL \ COMPOUND 9 Vehicle NORMAL \ COMPOUND \ VEHICLE 25 Skeleton NORMAL \ SKELETON 33 Creature NORMAL \ SKELETON \ CREATURE 97 Type Checking Core Agent Properties Every agent has these fundamental properties: Identity Position and Physics Rendering CAOS Variables Carrying System The Classifier System Every agent carries a Classifier — the type identifier the engine uses to find scripts, look up agents, and route messages. It is the agent's "address" in the game's type space. The Four Numbers In the original engine the classifier is four unsigned integers: Field Meaning Example ------- --------- --------- Family Broadest grouping. Family is reserved for all creatures. = creature, = food, = plant… Genus Subdivision of a family. For creatures: =Norn, =Grendel, =Ettin ( / / ). Norn = Species The most specific identifier — a unique agent kind. For creatures this carries the sex ( =male, =female). A specific toy, or male = Event The script number to run (e.g. 1=activate1, 2=activate2). Only meaningful during script lookup, not stored on a live agent's identity. A classifier is read left to right, broad to narrow: Family narrows to Genus, which narrows to Species. A complete agent type is the triple (e.g. a male Norn is ). Creature classifiers are built at birth as — which is why genus is 1-based (Norn=1) even though the genome stores it 0-based. The Catch-All Placeholder: 0 The value is never a real type — no agent is ever family 0, genus 0, or species 0. Instead, is a wildcard meaning "any value at this level." It exists so that a single generic script can serve many agents without having to be registered for every specific type. When the engine looks up a script for an agent, it does not require an exact match. It uses (mirrored in ), which falls back by progressively replacing the narrowest field with : Each step blanks the next field to the left, so the search only ever widens — it never tries or . Species is generalised first, then genus, then family. Why This Matters Shared behaviour with one script. A script installed as (family 2 = food, any genus, any species) runs for every food agent unless a more specific script overrides it. This is how whole categories share / behaviour. Global defaults. A script installed as is a last-resort handler that fires for any agent with no more specific script for event . Specificity wins. Because exact matches are tried first, a per-species script always overrides the genus- or family-level fallback. To specialise one agent kind, register a script at its full classifier; to cover the rest, register the broad or variant. Same rule for resource lookup. The identical species → genus → family widening is used for catalogue "Agent Help" tags ( ) and the CAOS command, so wildcard behaves consistently across scripts and resources. Pitfall: is only a wildcard in lookup/registration. A live agent's own always holds concrete non-zero values — you will never find a running agent whose family is . AgentHandle Reference System AgentHandles are smart pointers that safely reference agents. They use reference counting to prevent dangling pointers when agents are deleted. Why AgentHandles? Reference Counting Safe Accessors Exception Codes Code Meaning ------ --------- AHE0001 Null agent access AHE0002 Garbage agent access AHE0004-06 SimpleAgent type errors AHE0010-12 CompoundAgent type errors AHE0013-15 Vehicle type errors AHE0019-21 Creature type errors Agent Manager The AgentManager is the central registry for all agents in the world. Responsibilities Function Description ---------- ------------- Registration Track all active agents ID Assignment Generate unique agent IDs Lookup Find agents by ID, classifier, or position Update Loop Call agent updates each tick Garbage Collection Clean up deleted agents Spatial Queries Find agents in an area Agent Registration Spatial Queries Update Loop Agent Serialization Agents can be saved and loaded in binary format matching the original engine. Save Format Type-Specific Data Each agent subclass adds its own data: SimpleAgent: CompoundAgent: Parts array, base plane Vehicle: Cabin bounds, passengers Creature: Genome, brain, biochemistry Key Files File Purpose ------ --------- Base agent class (171 KB) Smart pointer system (16 KB) Agent registry (70 KB) Single-sprite agent Multi-part agent (31 KB) Passenger transport (12 KB) Related Articles Agent Types - Detailed type documentation Input & Output Ports - Agent communication Sprites & Display System - Rendering and animation

documents.content: Input & Output Ports The port system enables agents to communicate through signal-based connections, allowing creation of complex machine networks and interactive gadgets. Overview Ports are connection points on agents that can send and receive signals: Port Type Direction Purpose ----------- ----------- --------- InputPort Receiving Listens for signals, triggers scripts OutputPort Sending Broadcasts signals to connected inputs Connection Pattern InputPort Input ports receive signals and trigger script execution on their owning agent. Properties Key Features Property Description ---------- ------------- messageNumber CAOS script number triggered on signal excitementLevel Animated glow when receiving signals connectedPort Reference to connected OutputPort Connection Ownership InputPort controls the connection - this is a critical design decision: Script Triggering When a signal is received: OutputPort Output ports send signals to all connected input ports. Properties Signal Method Listener Management Port Base Class Both InputPort and OutputPort inherit from Port: PortBundle Each agent has a PortBundle that manages its ports. Structure Creating Ports Accessing Ports Cleanup Connection Flow Establishing Connection Signal Propagation CAOS Commands Creating Ports Connecting Ports Sending Signals Querying Ports Visual Feedback Ports have visual feedback for debugging and UI purposes. Excitement Levels Port Rendering Use Cases Machine Networks Connect multiple machines to create automated systems: Creature Interactors Objects that respond to creature actions: Daisy-Chaining One signal triggers multiple responses: Serialization Ports are saved and restored with world state. Binary Format Two-Phase Loading Phase 1: Create all ports (without connections) Phase 2: Restore connections after all agents loaded This ensures referenced agents exist before connecting. documents.title: Auto-Save and World Saving
documents.description: The invisible auto-save agent (classifier 1 2 7) that saves every 30 minutes, the Ctrl+R manual save, the deferred SAVE command, and the crash-safe World::Save() pipeline with .bak backups
documents.tags: autosave auto-save save savegame save game world save SAVE Ctrl+R tick 36000 timer 1 2 7 blnk TheWorldAndEverythingInIt SpaceAndAllThatIsOutThere backup bak CreaturesArchive mySaveNextTick saveNextTick World::Save saveWorld companion file sidecar bootstrap user interface
documents.content: Auto-Save and World Saving Overview Creatures 3 auto-saves the world every 30 minutes of running game time. Surprisingly, this is not engine code: the engine itself contains no save timer. Auto-save is implemented as an invisible CAOS agent installed by the bootstrap scripts, which periodically issues the command. The engine's only job is to honour that command by serializing the world at the start of the next tick. The save system therefore has two layers: The auto-save agent (game content, a bootstrap script) decides when to save. The engine save pipeline ( command → deferred flag → ) decides how the save happens. Both layers are present and functional in the web rebuild. The Auto-Save Agent (classifier 1 2 7) The agent is installed by the bootstrap scripts of both game packs: Pack Script ------ -------- Creatures 3 Docking Station The two scripts are functionally identical (the DS version just adds comments). The full script: Installation creates a simple agent with classifier family 1, genus 2, species 7 using the (blank) sprite gallery, so it has no visible appearance. It is one of several invisible "watcher" agents the bootstrap installs with the same pattern (agent help is 1 2 4, the keyboard handler is 1 2 6, the speech bubble factory is 1 2 10). sets the Invisible attribute — creatures cannot see or interact with the agent. sets the input event mask to raw key down, subscribing the agent to script 73. The timer: 36,000 ticks = 30 minutes arms the agent's timer. The world runs at 20 ticks per second (50 ms tick interval), so: Each time the timer fires, the agent's Timer script (event 9) runs, and it is a single command: No save immediately after loading Script 128 is the event, broadcast when a world has just been loaded. The agent responds with — re-arming the timer with its current rate ( as an rvalue returns the current timer rate). Re-arming resets the countdown, so after loading a world you always get a full 30 minutes before the first auto-save rather than inheriting whatever remained on the counter when the world was saved. Manual save: Ctrl+R Script 73 is the event ( carries the virtual key code). The handler checks for the R key with Ctrl held ( , VKCONTROL) and Shift not held ( , VKSHIFT). When Ctrl+R is pressed it saves immediately and resets the 30-minute countdown: So the effective behaviour is: the world saves 30 minutes after the last world load or manual Ctrl+R save, and every 30 minutes thereafter. Timing caveats The timer counts world ticks, not wall-clock time. If the world is paused (or the debugger is holding the tick loop), the countdown pauses with it. In the web rebuild, with enabled (the default), the simulation keeps ticking at full pace in hidden browser tabs — so auto-saves continue to fire every 30 real minutes even while the tab is not visible. How a Save Is Triggered: the SAVE Command The CAOS command does not save the world immediately. It only sets a flag: The application's main loop checks the flag at the start of the next tick and performs the actual save there: This deferred pattern lets the script that issued finish executing before the world is serialized. Scripts that combine saving with quitting or world switching must wrap the sequence in (e.g. ) so no other instruction interleaves between the scheduled operations. The web rebuild mirrors this exactly: ( ) calls , which sets . The game loop's scheduled-operation processing ( , ) performs the save at the start of the next tick and clears the flag. One rebuild-specific addition: scheduled saves/loads are deferred while any CAOS VM is suspended at a step-debug breakpoint, since destroying a paused VM mid-script would wipe the world during debugging. What Happens During the Save: World::Save() The original engine's ( ) performs a crash-safe, backed-up write: Record session metadata — the game end time and total length of play are stored. Resolve file paths inside the world's directory ( ): main save file (see naming below) — backup — temporary write target Back up the previous save — if is set (it is set only after an archive has been successfully loaded), the current save file is renamed to . This guarantees the file is always a version known to load correctly. Write to a temp file — the whole world is serialized through into the file. Atomically swap — only after a successful write is the old file deleted and the renamed into place. A crash mid-save can never destroy the existing save. Save file naming The main save file name is pack-dependent: Variant Save file --------- ----------- Creatures 3 Docking Station The single archive file contains the entire world state: the map, all agents and their VMs, creatures (genetics, biochemistry, brain, skeleton), game variables, message queues, and clock state. The web rebuild's saveWorld() ( ) follows the same sequence with web-specific plumbing: Concurrency guard — a flag rejects overlapping saves. Zoom reset — the camera zoom (a JS-only feature; the C++ engine has no zoom) is temporarily reset to 1:1 so camera and floating-agent positions are written in a form the original engine can load. Backup — mirrors the C++ logic via the world file API. Serialization — produces the binary archive buffer, byte-compatible with the original format. Storage backend — the buffer is written through : the Express backend writes it to on disk; the static (serverless) build writes to the browser's Origin Private File System (OPFS) instead. Progress display — like the C++ , the last presented frame is snapshotted and frozen behind the save progress popup. JS-only sidecar files Alongside the binary archive, the rebuild writes two optional JSON sidecars (both best-effort — a sidecar failure never fails the world save): File Contents Config gate ------ ---------- ------------- Engine version stamp, friendly CAOS script source, and debug metadata (default true) NornAI controller state — program banks, in-flight programs/drivers, debug history (default true) The original engine ignores unknown files in the world directory, so saves remain loadable in real Creatures 3 / Docking Station. Engine version stamp Every companion file carries an block recording the build that wrote the save, taken from the same metadata the in-app version display uses: On load the block is logged and stored on . Saves written before this stamp existed simply have no key ( is ), and a failed version lookup stamps rather than blocking the save. Summary of Save Triggers Trigger Mechanism --------- ----------- Every 30 minutes of running time Auto-save agent timer script ( ) issues Ctrl+R (Ctrl held, Shift not) Auto-save agent raw-key script ( ) issues and resets the timer World just loaded Auto-save agent ( ) resets the timer — no save, prevents saving right after load Any CAOS script The command schedules a save for the start of the next tick Related Files Game content: Original engine: — — handling in — Web rebuild: — the command — and scheduled-operation processing — and the binary serializer

documents.content: Creatures 3 Binary World Format Specification Overview This document describes the binary format used for Creatures 3 world save files ( files). The format is designed to serialize the complete game state including all agents, creatures, map data, scripts, and world settings. File Structure Compression Layer The world file uses zlib compression with a custom header: Data Types Reference Type Size Description ------ ------ ------------- int8 1 byte Signed 8-bit integer uint8 1 byte Unsigned 8-bit integer int16 2 bytes Signed 16-bit integer (little-endian) uint16 2 bytes Unsigned 16-bit integer (little-endian) int32 4 bytes Signed 32-bit integer (little-endian) uint32 4 bytes Unsigned 32-bit integer (little-endian) float32 4 bytes IEEE 754 single-precision float float64 8 bytes IEEE 754 double-precision float bool 1 byte Boolean (0 = false, non-zero = true) string 4 + n bytes Length-prefixed string (int32 length + chars) World Data Stream Hierarchy Object Serialization Protocol (OBST/OBEN) All complex objects are serialized using the OBST/OBEN marker protocol for handling circular references and object identity. Object Format Special Object IDs ID Constant Description ---- ---------- ------------- -2 NULLARCHIVEOBJECT Null/undefined object reference -1 NOTINARCHIVE Object not yet written to archive -3 RAWPOINTER Raw pointer (not managed) -4 FIRSTAGENT First agent marker >= 0 Back-reference or new object Index into objectVector Detailed Section Formats Scriptorium Map Manager CAOSVar (Game Variable Value) SYSTEMTIME Structure Message Creature History Agent Hierarchy Agent Serialization Format EntityImage Format Creature-Specific Data Creatures extend SimpleAgent and add extensive biological simulation data: Complete File Layout Sequence Diagram Object Reference Resolution The archive maintains two vectors for object identity: objectVector[] - Maps objectId (int32) to the actual object instance classVector[] - Maps classId (int32) to the class name string Resolution Process Example: Typical World File Statistics A typical Creatures 3 world file contains: Component Typical Count ----------- --------------- Compressed Size ~1 MB Decompressed Size ~8-9 MB Scripts 1,200+ MetaRooms 4-8 Rooms 200-400 Agents 1,000+ Creatures 1-10 Game Variables 50-100 Version History Version 12: Current format used by Creatures 3 and Docking Station Header includes compression library version info Full support for all agent types and creature biology Implementation Notes Endianness All multi-byte values are stored in little-endian byte order. String Encoding Strings are stored as length-prefixed with ASCII/Latin-1 encoding: Floating Point IEEE 754 format is used for all floating-point values. Compression zlib deflate compression is applied to the entire data stream after the header. Related Files - Binary read/write framework - World serialization - Agent collection management - Base agent serialization - Script storage - Map data serialization Document Version: 1.0 Last Updated: December 2024 Based on: analysis of the original Creatures 3 engine

documents.title: Genome Loading System
documents.description: Genome file structure and on-demand loading system
documents.tags: genome genetics format loading
documents.content: Creatures 3 Genome Loading System Overview This document explains how genome files ( ) are handled during world loading and creature operation. The key insight is that genome files are NOT embedded in the world save file - they are loaded on-demand from the folder. Key Principle: On-Demand Loading When a world is loaded from the binary file (e.g., ), the files in the folder are NOT loaded. Instead: The world file stores only moniker strings (e.g., ) The actual files are read on-demand when creature code needs genetic data This keeps world files smaller and allows genome sharing across worlds Data Flow Diagram Implementation Details GenomeStore Class The class maintains a list of moniker strings, not actual genome data: GenomeStore Serialization Only the moniker strings are saved to and loaded from the world file: Agent Serialization The GenomeStore is serialized as part of each Agent: On-Demand Genome Loading When creature code needs actual genome data, a temporary object is created that reads from the file: File Path Construction The genome file path is constructed from the moniker: When Are Genome Files Read? The files are read on-demand in various creature operations: After World Load - Remaking Skeleton Expressing Genes / Forming Body Parts Reading From Genome During Initialization Preloading Body Parts for Age Transition Design Benefits This on-demand loading design provides several advantages: Smaller World Files World saves only store moniker strings (~30 bytes each) Genome files can be 30-40 KB each A world with 10 creatures saves ~300 bytes instead of ~400 KB Genome Sharing Multiple creatures can reference the same genome file Cloned creatures share the parent's genome No data duplication in the world file Export/Import Compatibility Creature export includes genome in the file Import extracts genome to folder World file just needs to reference the moniker Crash Recovery Genome files are tracked via Orphaned genomes moved to on crash recovery See: World-Subfolder-System.md File Structure Moniker Format Monikers follow the format: where: First segment is typically the creature's name or "life"/"rain"/etc. Remaining segments are a unique hash Example: Genome File Contents The file contains the complete genetic data including: Header: Version, moniker, parent monikers Genes: All genetic instructions organized by type Brain genes (lobe definitions, tract connections) Biochemistry genes (reactions, receptors, emitters) Appearance genes (species, pigments, body parts) Organ genes Stimulus genes Instinct genes And many more... The genome is read and interpreted based on the creature's current: Sex: Determines which sex-linked genes are expressed Age: Determines which age-specific genes are active Variant: Selects between variant-specific gene alternatives Error Handling If a genome file is missing or corrupted: This is why the folder is critical - if the files are deleted but the world file references them, creatures will fail to load properly. Related Documentation - World file structure including GenomeStore serialization - How genome files are managed (creation, deletion, recovery) Key Components Component Purpose ------ --------- Moniker management, file path construction, serialization Genome loading from file, gene interpretation GenomeStore serialization as part of each agent On-demand genome loading for creature operations Gene expression for body parts Document Version: 1.0 Last Updated: December 2024 Based on: analysis of the original Creatures 3 engine

documents.content: CAOS Scripting Overview CAOS (Creatures Agent Object Script) is the scripting language that controls all agent behavior in Creatures 3. This article introduces the fundamentals of CAOS scripting. What is CAOS? CAOS is an event-driven scripting language where: Every object in the game is an agent Agents respond to events by running scripts Scripts are stored in the Scriptorium and looked up by classifier + event number A virtual machine (CAOSMachine) executes the scripts Key Concepts Concept Description --------- ------------- Agent Any interactive object (food, toys, machines, creatures) Classifier Identity triplet: family, genus, species Script CAOS code that runs in response to an event Event A trigger (timer tick, click, message, collision) Scriptorium Central registry storing all scripts Script Structure Basic Script Definition Script Components Part Description ------ ------------- Script start marker Broad category (1-65535) Sub-category (1-65535) Specific type (1-65535) Event number that triggers this script End of macro/script Event Numbers Events are numbered triggers that cause scripts to run. Standard Agent Events Event Name Description ------- ------ ------------- 0 Deactivate Agent deactivated 1 Activate1 Primary activation (click) 2 Activate2 Secondary activation 3 Hit Creature hit this agent 4 Pickup Agent picked up 5 Drop Agent dropped 6 Collision Wall/boundary collision 7 Bump Creature bumped agent 9 Timer Timer tick (TICK command) 12 Eat Agent eaten Creature Events Event Name Description ------- ------ ------------- 16-31 Extrovert Behaviors toward other agents 32-47 Introvert Self-directed behaviors 64-71 Involuntary Reflex actions (0-7) 72 Die Death script Message Events Event Name Description ------- ------ ------------- 100+ Custom User-defined message handlers System Events Event Name Description ------- ------ ------------- 120 SelectedCreatureChanged Active creature changed 128 WorldLoaded World finished loading 255 AgentException Error handler Context Variables When a script runs, special variables provide context about who triggered the script and who is being acted upon. Core Context Variable Description ---------- ------------- The agent that owns/runs this script The current target agent The agent that sent the message/stimulus First message parameter Second message parameter Iterator in ENUM loops Context Flow Example Usage The Scriptorium The Scriptorium is the central registry that stores all scripts, indexed by classifier and event number.
