documents.title: Touchscreen Support
documents.description: Auto-detection, gestures, on-screen keyboard, and floating-window touch handling for tablet play
documents.tags: touch touchscreen tablet iPad gesture pan tap two-finger keyboard soft keyboard InputManager FloatingWindow FloatingMenu pointer events
documents.content: Touchscreen Support The Web Rebuild plays on tablets and touch-capable laptops. When the engine detects a touch device it auto-enables touchscreen mode: gestures are translated to the engine's existing mouse and keyboard events so no game logic needs special-casing. This article documents how the detection works, the gesture mapping, and the on-screen options available in touchscreen mode. Activation: Auto-Detection Touchscreen mode is activated automatically by . A device is considered a touch device when both of these are true: The device exposes touch hardware — or . The primary pointer is coarse — . Requiring both conditions catches iPads, Android tablets, and Windows tablets while ignoring desktops or hybrid laptops with a precise mouse attached. The detected method is exposed via: → or → The current value is shown live in the Input tab of the debug console (right-hand "Current Input State" panel, top section labelled Input Method). Gesture Mapping All gestures are recognised on the game canvas and translated into the same / / / camera-pan events the engine already responds to. The recognizer lives in . Gesture Effect Engine event(s) --- --- --- One-finger drag Move the cursor at finger position (no buttons held) One-finger tap Left click then , button = 0 Two-finger tap Right click then , button = 2 Two-finger swipe (any direction) Pan the camera Direct Tap thresholds A touch counts as a tap (rather than a drag) only when both apply: Total duration ≤ 250 ms ( ) No finger has drifted more than 12 px from its start position ( ) If either threshold is exceeded the gesture is treated as a drag and no synthetic click is emitted at release. Two-finger pan details The world follows your fingers — i.e. swiping two fingers right pans the camera left, revealing more of the world to the right. The pan delta is computed from the centroid of the two touches between successive events and divided by the camera zoom so the perceived speed is consistent at any zoom level. Three or more simultaneous fingers cancel any pending tap. Adding a second finger during a one-finger drag promotes the gesture to a two-finger pan. Page scroll / pinch The canvas touch listeners are registered with and call on every touch event. This prevents the browser from scrolling the page or triggering pinch-to-zoom while you interact with the game. On-Screen Keyboard Button A keyboard glyph button ( ) appears just below the floating menu burger button only on touch devices. Tapping it summons the OS soft keyboard: Tap once to open the keyboard. Tap again to dismiss it. A green outline indicates the keyboard capture is currently focused. Internally this focuses a hidden 1×1 transparent element. The OS keyboard then dispatches normal / events to the document, where 's standard listeners pick them up. explicitly exempts the class so its focus does not suppress key delivery to the game. The button is created in and is hidden on desktops where a physical keyboard is always available. Floating Windows on Touch The minimap and the popout floating menu windows (Zoom, Speed, World) are draggable and resizable by touch as well as mouse. The titlebar and resize handle use Pointer Events ( / / ) with , so the same code path drives mouse, touch, and pen input. CSS on the titlebar and resize handle prevents the browser from hijacking the gesture for scrolling or pinch-zoom while you drag. What Is Not Yet Supported Pinch-to-zoom (use the +/− buttons in the floating menu). Long-press → right-click (use a two-finger tap). Edge scrolling (designed for a hovering mouse cursor, not touch). Implementation Files File Role --- --- Detection, gesture recognizer, synthetic mouse events, camera pan call, keyboard-capture focus exemption "Input Method" row in the Input debugger right panel Keyboard button creation, hidden capture input, conditional rendering Pointer-event drag and resize for all popout windows Verification Desktop (Chrome DevTools device emulation) — open the device toolbar, switch to iPad, reload the game. The Input debugger should show Input Method: Touch. Single-tap on the canvas to log a left-click; Alt-drag (DevTools two-finger simulation) to test the right-click; drag with two simulated fingers to pan the camera. Real touch device — confirm the keyboard button appears below the burger menu, opens the OS keyboard when tapped, and that typing produces events visible in the Input debugger. Desktop with a mouse — Input Method must read Mouse + Keyboard and the keyboard button must be absent. Existing arrow-key pan, middle-mouse drag, and wheel scroll behave exactly as before.

documents.description: Cross-platform Electron launcher for the Web Rebuild: prerequisites, installation, UI, configuration, and the role of the asset index files
documents.tags: launcher Electron desktop npm Node.js macOS Windows setup install npm install npm start electron-store config.json creatures3-launcher-config.json assetsDirectory port nodePath server backend health check asset-index.json asset-index-detailed.json generate-assets generate-asset-index Bootstrap prerequisites IPC preload contextBridge renderer main process
documents.content: Launcher The Creatures 3 Launcher is a small cross-platform desktop app (Electron) that replaces the manual terminal workflow for running the Web Rebuild. One window takes care of: checking Node.js, installing npm dependencies, picking an assets folder, generating the asset indexes the game needs to boot, starting and stopping the backend server, and opening the game in the system browser. It lives at and reads/writes a local JSON config so every settings survives between sessions. This article covers what the Launcher does, how to install and run it on Windows and macOS, what each configuration option means, and why the two files it can regenerate are essential for the game to start. Role and function Without the Launcher, a contributor has to do all of the following by hand, in the right order, from a terminal: Install Node.js. to get the backend's runtime dependencies ( , , ). to produce and in . (or ) to boot the backend. Open in a browser. The Launcher wraps each of those steps behind a status dot and a button, streams their output to a log panel, and persists the user's choices (port, assets directory, detected Node path) so the next launch is one click away. It's explicitly meant for developers and testers who want a friendly on-ramp without giving up the underlying scripts — every action the Launcher triggers is a process it spawns on top of the same scripts the terminal workflow uses. File layout The Launcher is completely independent of the game's tree — it has its own and its own dependencies. Prerequisites Node.js (required) Node.js is the only external dependency. It provides both the JavaScript runtime Electron needs and the CLI that installs the Launcher itself and the game's backend packages. Minimum version: Node.js or newer. LTS is recommended. The Launcher detects the system Node.js (not the one bundled inside Electron) by running on macOS or on Windows and then to confirm it works. The resolved path is cached in the config as and reused to spawn the backend server and the asset generator. macOS install options Installer (.pkg) — download the LTS build from and run it. Homebrew — . nvm — , then . If you use nvm, make sure a version is active in the shell you launch from. Windows install options Installer (.msi) — download the LTS build from . When asked, accept the "Tools for Native Modules" option. winget — . Chocolatey — . Verify either platform with: Game assets (required at runtime) The Launcher itself does not ship game assets. The actual Creatures 3 data files — sprites, sounds, backgrounds, genetics, bootstrap CAOS, etc. — must already be present under . The Launcher's Assets section lets you point at that directory and regenerate the index files the browser needs to find those assets (see Why asset index files are necessary). Installation Open a terminal (Terminal on macOS, Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows), then install the Launcher's npm dependencies from inside its folder: macOS Windows This pulls two packages declared in : (dev dependency) — the desktop framework. It bundles its own Chromium renderer and Node.js runtime and is roughly a 200 MB download the first time. — a tiny library that persists the Launcher's settings to a JSON file with atomic writes, so a crash mid-save can't corrupt the config. All transitive dependencies end up under , which is gitignored. Running the Launcher From the same directory: runs under the hood — the dot tells Electron to load the app from the current working directory using as the entry point. An equivalent but longer form is . Do not run without the trailing dot; Electron then has no app to load and opens an empty default window. On the very first launch the Launcher will: Create in the Launcher directory with defaults. Detect the system Node.js and display its version. Check whether contains , , and , and expose an button if any are missing. Default the assets directory to and show whether / exist inside it. Every check and every spawned command logs into the Logs tab. The UI The main window has two tabs: Setup (where you configure and act) and Logs (where all child-process output is streamed). Setup — Prerequisites Node.js — green dot + version if found, red dot + "Download Node.js" link if not. The resolved binary is cached as and is what gets used to spawn the backend and the asset generator. Dependencies — green dot when all three backend packages ( , , ) are installed under . Red dot otherwise, with a list of the missing packages. The npm install button runs inside and streams its output to the log. Setup — Assets Directory — the assets folder. Defaults to . The Browse… button opens the native OS directory picker. The selected path is persisted as . Index status — two dots, one for each index file. Green if the file exists in the selected directory, red otherwise. They refresh after you change the directory or regenerate the index. Refresh Asset Index — runs from , which executes and produces the two JSON files. Note: the generator always writes to regardless of which directory is selected in the Launcher — the selection controls where the Launcher checks for the index files. Setup — Server Port — number input, default , range – . Auto-saved (debounced ~500 ms) as . If the server is already running when you change the port, a "Restart server to apply" note appears. Status — red (stopped), yellow (starting/stopping), green (running). Green is set only after the Launcher polls successfully (polls every second, 30 s timeout). Local URL / External URL — clickable and LAN-address equivalents, populated once the server is up. Start Server — spawns in with the configured environment variable. Output (including the health-check polling result) is streamed to the log. Stop Server — graceful kill first ( on macOS, on Windows). If the process hasn't exited after 5 seconds, it's force-killed ( / ). The flag ensures child processes are terminated too on Windows. Crash detection — if the server process exits while the Launcher believes it's running, the dot flips back to red with a "Crashed" status and the exit code is logged. Cleanup — closing the Launcher window always kills the server process if one is running. Setup — Game Launch Open Creatures 3 in Browser — opens in the system default browser via . Only enabled while the server status is green. Logs tab Scrollable dark-themed log with four filter tabs: All, Server, Commands, Launcher. Receives streamed output from: (channel ) the backend server process (channel ) the asset index generator (channel ) server lifecycle events (channel ) A Clear button empties the log. Configuration options User settings live in , created automatically on first run and managed by with atomic writes. The file is gitignored. Every change made through the UI is saved immediately; the Launcher rehydrates from it on the next start. Key Type Default Role --- --- --- --- string (absolute path) resolved to an absolute path Directory the Launcher checks for / . Only used for the Assets section's status dots; the index generator itself still writes into . number (1–65535) TCP port passed as env var to when the server is started, and used to build the Local/External URLs and the game-launch URL. string (absolute path) or until detection succeeds Cached path to the system Node.js binary. Used to spawn and the asset index generator so the Launcher doesn't have to re-resolve it every time. A minimal generated file looks like: You can edit the JSON by hand while the Launcher is closed, but the UI is the intended way — it keeps the file in sync with the running state (disabled buttons, dot colours, etc.). Why asset index files are necessary The browser cannot list the contents of a directory. When the game starts in the browser, it has no way to ask "give me every file under ". It can only fetch a specific URL. This is a fundamental limitation of the web platform: retrieves a known resource; there is no filesystem API that enumerates a folder served over HTTP. The rebuild solves this by pre-scanning at build/setup time and writing the result to two JSON files the browser can fetch like any other resource: — the compact index. Contains a directory tree with filenames, sizes, and the explicit Bootstrap loading order (the ordered list of directories the engine replays on startup). This is what most runtime systems read. — the same data plus a map with per-file metadata (absolute and relative paths, extension, modification time, etc.). Used by tools that need to inspect or enumerate specific files. Multiple engine modules rely on these files — notably , , and the shared helper. documents.content: Asset Packs The Web Rebuild loads everything it needs to run — sprites, music, sounds, genomes, bootstrap CAOS scripts, and save files — from the directory. Rather than mixing one fixed set of files in that directory, the engine organizes them into asset packs: each pack is a self-contained subdirectory of holding a complete, independent version of the game's data. At startup the engine decides which pack to load, either automatically, from configuration, or by asking the user. This lets a single installation hold several game versions side by side — for example a clean Creatures 3 pack, a modded variant, or an experimental data set — and switch between them without copying files around. Because each pack also owns its own worlds and journals, switching packs gives you a fully isolated game state. This article explains the directory layout, how a pack becomes "valid", how the active pack is chosen at boot, how that choice flows through the frontend and backend so every path resolves inside the chosen pack, and how to add a new pack of your own. Directory layout The directory contains one subdirectory per pack. The pack name is the directory name (spaces allowed): A few directories deserve emphasis because they make a pack genuinely standalone: holds the scripts that build a fresh world. Its presence is what marks a subdirectory as a candidate pack. , , , are user data. They live inside the pack, so saves created while one pack is active never collide with another pack's saves. is a small sidecar directory the backend uses for per-pack UI settings ( ), console settings, and graph layouts. The is rendered as the pack's thumbnail on the chooser screen. The engine prefers and otherwise uses the first it finds in the pack. What makes a pack "valid" Two levels of recognition matter: Term Condition Consequence --- --- --- Candidate The subdirectory contains a folder The Launcher lists it; the engine knows it could be a pack Valid The candidate also contains both and The engine will offer it in the chooser and can boot it A candidate without its two index files is shown in the Launcher with a "No index" badge but is not selectable in the in-game chooser — generate its index first (see Adding a new pack). The index files are required because the browser cannot list a directory; the game reads to discover the files inside the pack. Choosing the active pack at startup When the game boots ( ), the very first step — before any asset-consuming system is constructed — resolves which pack to use. The logic lives in ( ), and applies these rules in order: Configured pack. If the GlobalConfig string (or the URL parameter ) names a valid pack, use it and skip the chooser. Single pack. Otherwise, if exactly one valid pack exists, use it automatically (no chooser). Multiple packs. Otherwise, show a tile chooser overlaid on the loading screen — one tile per valid pack, with its thumbnail and name. The boot sequence resumes when the user clicks a tile. No packs. If no valid pack exists, the loading screen shows an error (and, if candidates exist without indexes, hints to generate them). Configuration The active pack is controlled by a single GlobalConfig string: Mechanism Example Effect --- --- --- Config default Empty → run the rules above (chooser when multiple, auto when one) Config file Pin a pack in URL parameter Pin a pack per-load; overrides the config file Runtime Programmatic An empty string is the default and means "ask" (subject to the single-pack auto-select). A non-empty value that matches a valid pack skips the chooser; a value that doesn't match falls back to the chooser/auto rules with a console warning. How the choice propagates A chosen pack has to affect two layers: the browser (sprites, sounds, bootstrap, genomes — served as static files) and the backend (worlds, journals, PRAY resources, settings — read and written through Node). Both layers funnel through a single source of truth, so the pack is applied in exactly one place on each side. Frontend — PathResolver Almost every asset path in the browser is derived from ( ). Once a pack is chosen, calls , after which returns a pack-qualified path: , , , / , the body-part and gallery loaders, and the sound manager all build their paths off , so making PathResolver pack-aware steers every static fetch into the chosen pack with no per-consumer change. The pack must be set before is constructed — which is exactly why runs as the first boot step. Backend — ASSETSROOT and the active pack treats as the root ( , overridable via the environment variable) and tracks a single mutable . A single valid pack auto-activates at startup; otherwise the backend waits for the client to choose. When the frontend resolves a pack it calls , which re-points every per-pack service at : — worlds/saves ( , , , all follow it) / / — the per-pack settings sidecars — CAOS / journal I/O (a static class, so it uses a static settable base) — re-indexes the new pack's / / The net effect: after selection, saving a world writes to , journal writes land in , and PRAY resolves resources from the active pack. Single-pack-per-process. The backend holds one active pack at a time, which suits the single-user local model. If two browser tabs selected different packs, the last selection wins. REST API The pack endpoints are mounted at ( , backed by ): Endpoint Purpose --- --- List candidate packs as , plus the current pack Return the current active pack name Serve a pack's (used as the chooser thumbnail) → validate and re-point all per-pack services The asset index generator The two files are produced by (a CommonJS because the repo's root is ). It is pack-aware: The generator scans the pack, writes a file/directory listing plus a bootstrap loading order, and stamps the internal field as . Regenerate a pack's index after adding, renaming, or removing files inside it. The Launcher The Electron Launcher is pack-aware and is the easiest way to manage packs: The Assets section lists every candidate pack found in the configured assets directory, each with its icon and a valid / "No index" badge. Each pack has a Generate Index (or Regenerate Index) button that runs the generator for just that pack and flips it to valid on success. A Refresh button rescans the directory so a newly added pack folder appears without restarting the Launcher. The Launcher passes its configured assets directory to the backend as when it starts the server, keeping the two in sync. The Launcher only lists and generates — it does not pick a pack. Selection always happens in-game via the chooser (or the config / parameter). Adding a new pack Create a new subdirectory under , e.g. , and populate it with the game data ( , , , , , , , , …). At minimum it needs a folder to be recognized as a candidate. Add an icon, ideally , so it shows a thumbnail in the chooser. Generate its index — either click Generate Index in the Launcher, or run . This produces the two required index files and makes the pack valid. Boot the game. With more than one valid pack the chooser appears; pick My Mod**, or pin it with or . Saves, journals, and imported agents you create while the pack is active stay inside , fully isolated from other packs. Key files File Role --- --- Resolves the pack at boot; renders the chooser; applies the choice / pack-qualified — frontend source of truth The string and parameter , the active pack, and re-pointing The endpoints and pack discovery Pack-targetable asset-index generator Lists packs, generates per-pack indexes, Refresh button See also Launcher — the desktop app that lists packs and generates their indexes

documents.content: Configuration Options (GlobalConfig) The Web Rebuild centralises every development and tuning setting in a single system called GlobalConfig. Instead of scattering flags across modules, each system reads the values it cares about from at runtime. This article explains what that system is, the role of the file, the three ways to set a value, and then gives a complete reference for every configurable option, its default, its URL parameter (if any), and what it actually does. What GlobalConfig is is a small singleton defined in . It is a plain (non-module) script that attaches itself to so that any code — ES6 modules, non-module libraries, or the browser console — can read it without import gymnastics: The object holds one big nested object. The whole tree of defaults lives in the constructor; those defaults are the lowest priority and are what you get if you set nothing. Always read settings through optional chaining. GlobalConfig loads very early, but defensive code should still tolerate its absence: . Read settings at runtime (each time you need them) rather than caching them once in a constructor, so a console takes effect immediately. Priority order A setting can come from three places. Higher priority wins: URL parameters — highest priority, ideal for one-off testing ( ). They override everything for that page load. The config file ( ) — your persistent, file-based overrides. Fallback defaults — baked into . This order is implemented in the constructor: it first builds the defaults, then merges (the config file), then applies URL parameters last so they win. The config file: role and usage What it is for is where you keep development settings that you want to persist across page loads without editing engine code. It defines a single global, , whose shape mirrors the GlobalConfig tree. Anything you put there is deep-merged over the defaults; anything you omit keeps its default. Where it lives and how it loads The root loads the file before , which is why can pick it up during construction: There are up to three file locations, by directory. None are tracked in git — each is a personal, local override: Path Loaded by ------ ----------- the main game page ( ) test pages pages All three are gitignored, so your settings stay local. The first time you set up the project, create by copying the template (see below); if the file is absent the engine simply runs on the defaults. For one-off experiments you don't want to persist at all, prefer URL parameters. The template is a generated reference that enumerates every GlobalConfig key set to its default value, with inline comments. It is the one file in this set that is tracked, and it is kept in sync with the object in . To bootstrap your own config, copy it to the gitignored for the page you run, delete the blocks you don't care about, and edit the rest: One important override on the main page The root force-enables three loading flags immediately after loads, regardless of what your config file says: So on the main game page these three flags are always — the style overrides only take effect on the lightweight test pages that don't apply this guard. Keep this in mind when a in your config file appears to be ignored on the main page; that is by design. How to set an option You have three interchangeable mechanisms. URL parameter (one-off, highest priority) Boolean params expect the literal strings / . Numeric params are parsed with / . Only the parameters listed in the reference below are recognised. Config file (persistent) Edit as shown above. Survives reloads, no code changes to the engine. Flip a boolean and return the new value. Deep clone of the entire current config. Restore all settings to the baked-in defaults. List settings that differ from defaults. Build a query string for the current non-default settings. Print a quick usage cheatsheet. Configuration reference Every option below is addressed by its dot-path (e.g. ). The Default column is the value from . documents.content: Web Rebuild Configuration Files Beyond the game data it shares with the original engine (worlds, creatures, journals), the Web Rebuild persists a small set of JS-only configuration files. These files store your preferences — window positions, volume, graph layouts, debug-console filters — rather than game state. They are written in plain JSON, are never read or written by the original engine, and are safe to inspect, copy, or delete (deleting one simply resets the corresponding settings to defaults). This article catalogues each file: where it lives, what it contains, which part of the engine reads and writes it, and how to back it up. The per-pack sidecar directory The main home for these files is a directory named created automatically inside the active asset pack: Key properties: Per-pack. The backend re-points these files whenever the active asset pack changes, so your Creatures 3 and Docking Station settings are fully independent (see Asset Packs for how the active pack is resolved). Created on demand. The subdirectory is created on every read or write if missing — you never need to create it yourself. Deliberately segregated. The directory keeps JS-only data out of the engine-shared world directories, so a pack's game data stays byte-compatible with the original engine. 💾 Back up this directory. If you reinstall, move, or re-import your assets, copy each pack's folder somewhere safe and restore it afterwards — it is the only durable copy of your UI, graph, and console preferences. How persistence works (localStorage + server sync) Each file is the server-side half of a two-way sync with the browser's : At startup, the frontend fetches the server snapshot and applies it to before any UI module reads its persisted state. The server copy is authoritative at startup — settings survive a browser-storage reset. If the server has no copy yet, the current values are uploaded to bootstrap it. During play, remains the primary store. Writes to tracked keys are pushed back to the server (debounced for UI settings, on explicit save for the graph layout). Degrades gracefully. If the backend is unreachable, keeps working standalone and the sync silently retries on the next session. The whole mechanism is gated by one GlobalConfig flag, (default ; see Configuration Options). Setting it to disables all server sync and leaves settings purely in the browser. and follow this envelope shape: uses a per-device envelope instead — see the next section. The three settings files — general UI preferences --- --- Written by via Frontend sync (debounced interceptor) Stores pure user-preference UI state, partitioned per device. Window positions are absolute pixels, so a layout saved on a desktop must not be applied to a tablet — each browser profile mints a stable random id (localStorage key , never synced) and reads/writes only its own bucket (format v2): A device the server has never seen starts from defaults (always in-viewport) and gets its own bucket on first save. Clearing browser storage mints a new device id; orphaned buckets are pruned (the newest 10 are kept). Legacy single-bucket v1 files are superseded on the first save after updating — every device starts fresh once. excerpts.introduction: Introduction to Creatures 3 Web Rebuild Welcome to the documentation for the Creatures 3 Web Rebuild project - a faithful recreation of the classic 1999 life simulation game in modern JavaScript. About Creatures 3 Creatures 3 was developed by Creature Labs (formerly Cyberlife Technology) and released in 1999. It features sophisticated artificial life simulation with: Digital Creatures - AI-controlled beings (Norns, Grendels, Ettins, Geats) with complex neural networks, genetics, and biochemistry
excerpts.creature-species: Norns, Grendels and Ettins Creatures 3 ships three playable species — Norns, Grendels and Ettins. They are not three creature systems. They are one system, run three times over three genomes: the same faculties, the same brain layout, the same 256-chemical bloodstream, the same seven life stages, the same twenty drives. Everything that makes a grendel a grendel rather than a norn is written in its DNA — a handful of extra reactions, a different set of birth chemicals, different rewards attached
